title: Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding
authors: Elisabeth Kirsten, Annalina Buckmann, Abraham Mhaidli, Steffen Becker
text: QDA (QDA) is an approach used in HCI (HCI) research to analyze unstructured data, such as interview data or responses to open-ended survey questions. A fundamental step in QDA is coding, the systematic process of identifying, annotating, and categorizing data segments based on recurring themes and patterns, and assigning according categories or “codes” [1,2,3,4,5]. Coding data can be a time-consuming process, particularly when analyzing large volumes of data (e. g., tens of thousands of open-ended survey responses). The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence, and in particular LLM (LLM) (e. g., GPT-4 [6], Gemini [7], or Llama 2 [8]) could significantly speed up the coding process, yet their value and validity needs to be evaluated. LLM have demonstrated remarkable performance in annotation tasks in zero-shot or few-shot learning scenarios where no or little labeled data is given [9,10,11]. As these models become integral to HCI research, it is imperative to critically evaluate their potential benefits and risks, as well as methodological challenges associated with the integration of LLM. In this workshop submission, we present the preliminary results of a study scrutinizing how LLM perform at applying tags for QDA in coding tasks of different complexity. Specifically, we explore LLM -assisted QDA of a real-world dataset to understand how LLM perform, how they compare to human coders, and how their performance is affected by the type of coding (e. g., semantic vs. latent themes [1]). First, we develop a strategy for prompting LLM to apply tags for QDA. We then implement this strategy with GPT-3.5 [12] and GPT-4 [6] on interview data and compare the models’ performance with human coding in three tasks that require different levels of interpretation.
